text:
COPART $CPRT PAID $1.9 BILLION TO STOP DEPENDING ON CAR CRASHES - SIX LEN5ES, SIX NAMES:

Six Len5es, six names, and what they share is not an industry. Every one is paid by repetition - a filter that clogs, a toolbox bought on installments, a shift that needs covering, a loan that rolls over, a ham. The verdict on the name at the top: a record share of damaged cars is now written off, Copart handled fewer of them anyway, and Thursday night's $1.9 billion is the company conceding that its own repetition is slowing.

Copart at $31.82 (after hours), +$1.87 / +6.24% from Friday's $29.95 close, after a regular close of $31.72, +$1.77 / +5.91%. The Dallas company runs the online auctions where insurers sell cars they have decided are not worth repairing.

Reported after the close on Thursday, September 10, for the three months to July 31: revenue $1.15B, +2.4%; profit $0.35 a share, -14.6%, against the $0.38 carried; cars sold worldwide -2.9%, US insurance volumes -7.5%, average price +3.5%. Dearer cars covering for fewer cars. Total loss frequency - the share of damaged cars an insurer junks instead of repairing - hit a record 23.3% for a June quarter against 22.4%, and still did not help, because collision claims fell 3.4% in a year.

So that same night Copart agreed to buy ACV Auctions at $10.41, unchanged today, for $10.50 a share in cash. ACV sells no wrecks. It runs the dealer-to-dealer market in trade-ins and off-lease cars with clean titles, over 800,000 a year, and in chief executive Jay Adair's words "operates with virtually no land of its own." Copart sold more than 4 million cars out of hundreds of physical yards. It is buying its own opposite. ACV fits none of the six styles weighed here, its price now simply the offer.

WATCH the domestic insurance car count, not revenue. WHEN: the tender offer - the formal invitation to ACV holders to sell - must open within seven business days of Thursday's agreement, with closing expected by end-December; first-quarter results are tentatively November 19. RISK: ACV trades nine cents under the offer, and a $115.3M reverse termination fee is what Copart owes if regulators block it.

MOMENTUM LEN5:
ManpowerGroup at $59.15 (after hours), +$2.69 / +4.76% from Friday's $56.46 close; the regular day ended $58.03. The Milwaukee firm finds people work and bills the employer. Fifth of thirty; this Len5 wants the recent and longer climbs to agree near a one-year high, and only the longer does: +135% off February's $25.15 low but 7.4% under August 28's $63.88. July 16: revenue $4.9B, +8%; $0.99 a share with one-off items set aside, against a $1.44 loss a year ago. CHANGE IT: a close above $63.88, or a third quarter under the $1.01 carried for October 15. VERDICT: a bet on other firms hiring, already priced for the recovery it describes.

QUALITY-VALUE LEN5:
Copart again, third of fifty-four, weighed rather than repeated. This Len5 wants a business nobody could rebuild, bought under its worth. The rebuild half is not arguable: licensed yards outside every American city, plus the insurer contracts to fill them, is not something a rival assembles. The price half is 19.3 times profit, 35.0% under last September's $48.96. Third rather than first is the cheque just written, which tops the $1.48B earned all fiscal year and leaves just over $2B of the $4.5B held, still with no borrowings. CHANGE IT: domestic insurance cars rising again with no purchase inside the number.

DEEP-VALUE & SPECIAL-SITUATIONS LEN5:
Donaldson at $87.93 (after hours), -$1.32 / -1.48% today. The Minneapolis firm makes the filters that keep dirt out of engines and factory air. Fifth of fifty-one; this Len5 wants settled earning power cheaply, and a filter is settled by design: sell the housing, then the replacements for the machine's life. August 26: sales $1,058.8M, +8.0%, of which replacement filters were $511.6M, +9.4% - about half the company and its fastest-growing part. CHANGE IT: the aftermarket slipping while new equipment carries the $4.22-$4.38 mapped for fiscal 2027; tentatively December 3. VERDICT: 23.2 times profit is full price for a filter maker, hence fifth.

GROWTH LEN5:
U.S. Bancorp at $62.82 (after hours), -$0.02 / -0.03% today. The Minneapolis bank takes deposits, lends, and processes card payments for shops. First of thirty on a Len5 wanting growth the price has not charged for, and 12.5 times profit is the lowest price here. July 16: net income $2,177M, +20%; $1.35 a share, +22%, against $1.27 carried - a seventh straight quarter above it - with fee income +13.2% growing faster than lending's +7.5%. CHANGE IT: the Federal Reserve decides Wednesday, September 16 at 2:00pm ET from a range of 3.50%-3.75% unmoved all year, and a bank's net interest margin - what it keeps on loans after paying depositors, 2.79% here - moves first. VERDICT: that growth at that price, paying 3.4% a year, ex-dividend September 30.

HYPERGROWTH LEN5:
Wise at $12.13 (after hours), +$0.11 / +0.92% today. The Jersey company runs the app for sending money abroad without a bank's exchange-rate markup. Sixth of thirty on a Len5 wanting a business early as well as fast. Fast is settled - July 16: net revenue $714.0M, +25%, on $69.3B moved across borders, +26%. Early is the odd half, because Wise is becoming something else: transaction fees were $540.9M of that revenue, customers now leave $41.2B parked in their accounts earning $225.4M of interest, and activity other than sending money abroad is 51% of the total. CHANGE IT: central banks write that interest line, not Wise, so transfers must grow fast enough to carry a rate-cutting cycle; Wise set October 15. VERDICT: 24.6 times profit, and over half the business is no longer the thing Wise is for.

INCOME LEN5:
Smithfield Foods at $20.31 (after hours), +$0.05 / +0.25% today, after a one-year low of $20.05 on Friday. The Virginia company raises hogs and makes packaged pork. Fourth of thirty on a Len5 wanting cash reaching owners that the business itself funds: $0.3125 a quarter, $1.25 a year, about 6.2% here, much the largest yield on this board, with borrowings net of cash at only 0.4 times a year's cash profit. The cash is the objection. August 11, first half: a record $638M of adjusted operating profit, yet running the business produced $204M, $165M went into plant and equipment, and the $39M left sits against roughly $246M of dividends. CHANGE IT: the second half is when hams sell, so a full year where spare cash covers the payment; tentatively October 27. VERDICT: the yield is real and the first half did not earn it in cash.

Americans crash less often now, and wreck cars more expensively when they do. Copart has spent 44 years perfecting the second half of that sentence and has no answer to the first. On Thursday it paid $1.9 billion for one, and competition regulators decide whether it gets to keep it.

COLLEGE FOOTBALL BETTING INTEL — NORTHERN ILLINOIS at ARIZONA — Saturday, Sept. 19, 10:30 ET

CONFIRMED: ARIZONA’S LEADING RECEIVER GIOVANNI RICHARDSON WILL MISS AT LEAST ONE GAME WITH A LOWER-BODY INJURY.

Richardson was injured during Arizona’s 28-17 loss to BYU and has now been ruled out for the Northern Illinois game.

The sophomore had emerged as Arizona’s clear No. 1 receiving option, leading the Wildcats with 14 receptions for 161 yards through two games. He caught five passes for a team-high 48 yards against BYU before leaving in the second quarter.

The distribution gap is meaningful: no other Arizona player has more than seven receptions this season.

Rodney Gallagher III should see an expanded role after catching five passes against BYU, while freshman Caleb “Jet” Smith is another candidate for additional targets.

MARKET MOVE: Arizona opened approximately -35.5 and is now generally -34 to -34.5, with a total around 49.5.

The one-point move toward Northern Illinois is directionally consistent with Richardson’s absence, although it cannot reliably be attributed entirely to the injury.

Betting implication: Richardson’s loss matters more to Arizona passing efficiency, receiver props and team-total markets than it does to the full-game spread because Northern Illinois is such a large underdog.

Arizona’s offense noticeably deteriorated after Richardson exited against BYU, getting shut out in the second half. Against an NIU team that has struggled badly, Arizona can still dominate without him, but covering a number in the mid-30s requires sustained offensive production.

The market has already shaved roughly a point from Arizona’s opener, so the injury should not be treated as undiscovered information.

text:
Faster Growth Still Leaves a Debt Problem

Scott Bessent’s 3% growth argument offers Washington an attractive possibility: expand the economy fast enough to make a heavy debt burden easier to carry.

The difficulty for bondholders is that a larger economy can improve the outlook while leaving the government’s borrowing requirement high enough for debt to keep rising relative to output.

Improvement is not stabilization

The Wall Street Journal analysis describes a CBO-based productivity scenario that raises growth to 2.4% and puts debt at 109% of GDP after a decade, versus a 120% baseline.

The ratio is lower than the baseline, but it continues climbing under that scenario, so the result illustrates relief rather than a completed fiscal repair.

These are conditional projections, not measured outcomes or a promise that AI adoption will generate the assumed productivity gain.

Bessent’s preferred growth rate also needs to be sustained, which makes a strong quarter or a burst of investment inadequate evidence that the fiscal path has changed.

The interest-cost catch

Higher productivity can lift tax receipts, but it can also increase investment demand and interest rates, raising the cost of servicing outstanding debt.

The WSJ analysis says higher debt-service costs consume more than one-third of the additional revenue in the CBO-based scenario.

That interaction matters because the government already carries a large debt stock, making the price of borrowing an important offset to the benefits of faster output.

An aging population adds another constraint, limiting labor-force expansion and leaving productivity to do more of the work needed to sustain faster growth.

The bond-market test

My read is that an AI productivity boom strengthens the fiscal outlook without automatically removing Treasury supply or refinancing pressure from the investment case.

Evidence of improvement would include durable productivity gains, stronger revenues relative to spending and a structural budget gap that actually narrows.

If growth accelerates while the borrowing requirement remains large, investors could still demand compensation for financing costs and the uncertainty around future fiscal adjustment.

Bottom line

Growth can make the debt burden more manageable, but a scenario with a smaller, still-rising debt ratio does not justify treating fiscal risk as solved.

COINBASE $COIN GAINED $4.3 BILLION TODAY ON A VOTE THAT HAPPENS TOMORROW AT 2:15PM:

Coinbase at $188.10 (after hours), +$12.84 / +7.33% from Friday's $175.26 close, after finishing the regular day at $191.44, +$16.18 / +9.23%. The New York company, 4,951 employees, founded 2012, runs the biggest cryptocurrency exchange in the United States and takes a fee on every trade.

The verdict: nothing happened to this business today. A bill got a new draft, an analyst who had the stock at Sell moved to Neutral, and the market paid about $4.3 billion for the pair - $46.2B of company on Friday, $50.5B tonight.

Sunday night, Senate Republicans released a revised draft of the CLARITY Act, the bill that would settle which American regulator supervises digital coins: the Securities and Exchange Commission for anything counted as a security, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission for everything else. The new text takes in 126 changes Democrats asked for. Tomorrow, Tuesday September 15 at 2:15pm ET, the Senate votes on whether to begin formally debating it at all - 60 votes needed, against 53 Republican seats, so at least seven Democrats or independents have to cross. Two did in May, when the Senate Banking Committee moved it along 15-9. And the vote does not pass the bill. It decides whether the Senate may argue about it.

Separately, Compass Point analyst Ed Engel raised Coinbase from Sell to Neutral, target price $177 from $130. Read that twice: the upgrade is to Neutral, and the target sits $11.10 below where the shares trade tonight.

One figure frames the day. Polymarket, where people bet real money on outcomes, prices the CLARITY Act becoming law this year near 30% - up hard from about 12% earlier this month, so the draft moved something real, and still a market saying the thing most likely does not happen.

The business went the other way. July 30, after the close, for the three months to June 30:

- Net revenue $1.22B against $1.50B a year earlier - about 18% less money coming in
- Trading fees $599M, down 21% from the previous three months
- Subscriptions and services $555M, the largest share of the total that half has ever carried, still 12% below a year ago
- A net loss of $359.5M, where analysts had carried $0.14 a share of profit
- Cash profit before interest, tax and wear on equipment: $207.8M, a fourteenth straight positive quarter

Three quarters running have now filed a loss: $666.7M, then $394.1M, then $359.5M. That is $1.42B, and it leaves no profit in the last twelve months.

One line points the other way, and it is the real case for owning this. Coinbase handled a record 10.3% of the world's crypto trading last quarter, up from 9.1% three months before, on $146.4B of trades. It is winning a bigger share of a shrinking pot.

Now the part nobody cheering today has priced. The same draft hands the Treasury secretary power to temporarily restrict stablecoin rewards if they start pulling deposits out of small community banks. Stablecoins are digital dollars, each meant to be backed one-for-one by a real dollar; Coinbase pays people to hold them and earns interest on the pile, and that income sits inside the subscriptions line - close to half of all revenue. Average USDC held on its platform hit $20B last quarter, more than 30% of every one in existence. The bill Coinbase spent today celebrating carries a switch pointed at its own engine.

Two prices say today was about Washington, not crypto. Bitcoin sits at $78,390, +$830 / +1.07% since midnight. Robinhood Markets at $113.93 (after hours), +$1.36 / +1.21% from Friday's $112.57 close, is the other place Americans buy coins in an app; it closed the regular day +1.55%. Coinbase closed +9.23%. Same session, same asset, three different answers. Robinhood is on none of the six Len5es either, and price is why: at about 50 times the last year of profit and 10.7 times book value - what owners would keep after selling everything and paying every debt - neither value Len5 is offered a discount.

This was not just a morning pop. The stock opened at $180.98, already $5.72 / +3.26% up before a share traded in the session, then added another $10.46 across the day on 13.2M shares against a two-week average of 8.1M.

VERDICT: a much higher price for a company that has lost money three quarters running, bought on a probability rather than a result. Coinbase is not a pick on any of the six Len5es, and the reason is arithmetic rather than opinion - both value Len5es need profit to divide a price by and there is none, the Len5 hunting businesses that are early as well as fast gets a $50.5B company with revenue going backwards, and there is no dividend for the Income Len5 to count. Momentum is the near miss: $188.10 sits 35.2% above the $139.11 low of July 31, the recent half of that test, while the $402.16 set on October 10 last year flatly disagrees, leaving the stock 53.2% under it. A filed profit changes the value reads; a run back toward that high changes the momentum one.

WATCH the share of revenue that is not trading fees, not the coin price - that half is near fifty cents on the dollar, and the stablecoin income inside it is what the new bill can reach. WHEN: tomorrow, 2:15pm ET; third-quarter results are tentatively Thursday, October 29, after the close, with a $0.16 loss carried. RISK: at 3.5 times book value with no earnings underneath, a failed vote takes back the only thing that was bought today.

A trading day is meant to tell you what a business is worth. Today it told you what a hundred senators might do at a quarter past two tomorrow afternoon, and charged $4.3 billion for the guess. In the same quarter, Coinbase sold less, lost money, and won more of the market than it ever has. None of those three is what moved.

@JMeservey your final question was very, very important: why should the United States recognize Somaliland, rather than keep the status quo?

The United States already has established relationships and significant military infrastructure in the region. One of its most important bases in Africa is Camp Lemonnier in Djibouti. It also has a presence in Somalia, including at Baledogle Airfield. These facilities give the U.S. access, logistics, and operational reach in the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea.
The point is the United States already has working arrangements with Djibouti and Somalia that cover much of what Somaliland is pitching. Recognition of Somaliland would almost certainly damage relations with Somalia, strain ties with Djibouti, and create problems with other East African and African Union states, Arab League that treat Somaliland as part of Somalia. In practice, Washington would be choosing between Somaliland and a larger set of existing partners.

That is why the status-quo question was very important. Recognition is not only about whether Somaliland is stable or strategically located. Puntland State is stable and can offer everything that Somaliland has to offer but it is also about what the United States would risk losing in Djibouti, Somalia, and the wider region.

🚔 Plymouth Girl, 17, Thrown From Car After Fighting Off Assault Attempt
🗞️ Wilkes-Barre Times Leader · September 14, 1926 · Page 1

Wilkes-Barre police are searching today for a young man accused of attempting to sexually assault a 17 year old Plymouth girl before throwing her from his automobile early this morning.

Anna Felnock, 17, of 712 Temperance Hill, Plymouth, left home around 6:30 a.m. for her job at the Palace Laundry on North Washington Street. While waiting for a bus at Carey Avenue and Division Street, a young man driving a Ford coupe offered her a ride into town.

Felnock accepted. Instead of taking her directly to the Square, however, the driver traveled along Carey Avenue and Academy Street to South Franklin Street. Between South and Northampton streets, he stopped the car and allegedly attempted to assault her.

Felnock fought him off. The man then threw her from the automobile and sped away.

Charles Zimmer of 60 Davis Place and another man came upon Felnock lying in the street several minutes later. They carried her into the nearby home of Mrs. Frances Weaver, 105 South Franklin Street, and police were summoned.

Felnock was taken to Wilkes-Barre General Hospital suffering from bruises and contusions of the right knee and elbow, along with shock.

Captain Eckert of the traffic squad and Philip Eckert are searching for the driver. Felnock told police the man claimed to work somewhere on the “mountain,” and authorities believe that information may lead to his arrest.

Police called the case one of the worst of its kind reported to them in some time.

I am 100 percent Canadian. That makes me 100 percent North American. 🇨🇦🇺🇸🇲🇽Not European. Not “the most European of non-European countries.” Zero percent Brussels. Zero percent Strasbourg talking points.

Name one country on earth that would not want Canada’s geographic position: a shared continent, an integrated industrial base, and an imaginary line between us and the largest, richest market in the world. That is not a slogan. That is the country we actually live in.Carney can sell the European line to a room that already wants to hear it. His supporters will nod because it lets them feel worldly without looking at a map. They treat Canada like a finishing school for European manners: same flag, different continent, different neighbours, different problems. They lecture about values while the country that trades, works, freezes, and pays the bills on this side of the Atlantic is treated as an embarrassment to be managed.

Then they act shocked by the arithmetic.

About 72 percent of Canada’s goods exports still go to the United States. In some recent months that share has fallen into the mid-60s, not because Ottawa discovered a new continent, but because the relationship is being broken on purpose. Roughly three-fifths of our merchandise imports still come from the U.S. The honest point is simpler: we need that market far more than it needs ours. A trade war with your largest customer is not courage. It is a bet that slogans can replace customers.

Walking away from talks at the eleventh hour does not change that. Here is what happened. After weeks of negotiations, the talks collapsed late on the deadline. Washington said it had offered Canada the most preferential treatment of any major exporter. Ottawa said the last-minute terms were a bad deal, suspended negotiations, and sent its team home. Fine. Argue the terms. Do not pretend Canada can casually replace three-quarters of its export market with Europe and a press release.

And do not rewrite the scoreboard of that night. Foolish Liberals cheered as if Carney had just bodychecked the big bad orange man. Elbows up. Never 51. A hockey slogan instead of a customer.

More than eleven years ago, the United States was not treated as an enemy. It was treated as a partner. That is the relationship this country was built on. Now the same crowd that cannot look at a map wants to pick a fight with the market that keeps the lights on.

And do not even get me started on the outrageous immigration taking place while all of this is happening.

Some of us look at the pattern and draw a harder conclusion. Carney is in cahoots with Trump to cripple Canada until the only option left is for the United States to annex us. For me, it cannot happen soon enough. I am 100 percent Canadian. That makes me 100 percent North American.

Do not rewrite the economic scoreboard either. Canada was the only G7 country, and for a stretch the only G20 country, to slip into a technical recession: two straight quarters of shrinking GDP in late 2025 and early 2026. Growth has since ticked back up. That does not erase the damage: weak per-capita growth, businesses getting hit, companies uprooting to the States, and households falling further behind.

Meanwhile Ottawa boasts of more than $26 billion in aid to Ukraine since 2022. Food Banks Canada recorded nearly 2.2 million visits in a single month — the highest number they have ever counted. Visits have more than doubled since 2019. One in four people in this country now lives with food insecurity. You can support Ukraine and still notice that Canadians are lining up for groceries. A government that cannot hold both thoughts at once is not serious.

If the Canada they want is a European talking point with a maple-leaf sticker, they should say so. Stop wrapping a transatlantic rebrand in patriotism while the North American advantage — the one thing almost every other country would kill for — is being talked away.

Bob Russell

text:
The contract is where the deal is either protected or exposed.

10 C.A.R. forms California agents should understand:

RPA-CA — Residential Purchase Agreement
    The offer: price, deposit, loan terms, contingencies, escrow timing, possession, costs, included/excluded items.
RLA — Residential Listing Agreement
    Seller relationship: term, list price, compensation, MLS instructions, exclusions, marketing, broker authority.
BRBC — Buyer Representation and Broker Compensation Agreement
    Buyer relationship, term, compensation, broker duties, buyer duties, and exclusivity if selected.
SPQ — Seller Property Questionnaire
    Seller disclosures: repairs, defects, permits, water issues, insurance claims, legal issues, material facts.
TDS — Transfer Disclosure Statement
    Seller property condition disclosure and agent visual inspection section.
AVID — Agent Visual Inspection Disclosure
    What the agent visually observes. Not a contractor report. Not a home inspection.
CR — Contingency Removal
    Used when buyers remove loan, appraisal, investigation, sale of property, or other contingencies.
RR — Request for Repair
    Buyer requests repairs, credits, price changes, or corrections after investigation.
RRRR — Seller Response and Buyer Reply to Request for Repair
    Controls the repair negotiation.
COP — Contingency for Sale of Buyer’s Property
    Used when the buyer needs to sell another property to close.

Forms are not paperwork.

They control terms, timing, disclosure, leverage, risk, compensation, and expectations.

Know what you are putting in front of people.

Merck & Co. at $145.48 (after hours), +$1.55 / +1.08% today, and Moderna at $146.40 (after hours), +$2.43 / +1.69% today, said their INTerpath-001 trial worked: a cancer vaccine built individually for each patient, given with Keytruda, held melanoma off after surgery longer than Keytruda alone - the first of its kind to clear a late-stage trial. The sequencing that picks that vaccine's targets out of each patient's tumor is Personalis's work.

Tempus rose 24.1% that day and hit $72.69 by August 21. The best week of news in Personalis's history lifted its buyer by nearly half and lifted what Personalis owners collect by nothing. On July 17 that $16.25 meant 0.3097 Tempus shares; tonight it means 0.2621. And the stock has closed above $16.25 in sixteen of the seventeen sessions since August 20, as high as $18.38. A deal at a set value normally trades a shade under it; this one trades over. That is people paying for a raise nobody has offered.

Momentum is the Len5 watching it, second of thirty. That style wants a price near the top of its one-year range with the recent climb and the longer one agreeing, and both hold: $4.955 on April 29 up to $18.89 on August 21, today 13.8% under that. The engine is no longer its own. August 4 brought June-quarter revenue of $22.4M, +30%, the clinical test itself only $2.6M of it, and a loss widening to $0.30 a share from $0.23 - none of which moves this price now. CHANGE IT: Tempus's fifteen-day average slipping under $48.42, which turns a fixed value into a fixed share count and sends these owners downhill on somebody else's ride.

VERDICT: a real breakout whose remaining upside belongs to the buyer. WATCH the $16.25, not the test volumes; forecasts and quarterly calls stopped when the papers were signed. WHEN: no meeting date is set - the voting documents went in at the start of September, with a backstop deadline of April 20, 2027. RISK: about $76.8M is owed either way if this breaks. None of the other three is on a Len5: Tempus and Moderna are loss-makers, leaving the value styles no profit to divide a price by, and Merck at 115 times profit is the opposite complaint.

QUALITY-VALUE LEN5:
Arch Capital Group at $97.42 (after hours), +$1.33 / +1.38% today, runner-up of fifty-four, insures specialist risks and reinsures other insurers out of Bermuda. This Len5 wants a business nobody could rebuild bought under its worth, and the unbuyable part is refusing business at a bad price: on July 28 claims and costs took 83.5 cents of every premium dollar despite $201M of catastrophe losses, at 7.5 times profit. WATCH the tentative October 26 report, where $1.85 is carried against the $2.56 just earned - that gap is hurricane season, and it is the risk. VERDICT: the deepest discount here, priced for a bad autumn that has not come.

DEEP-VALUE & SPECIAL-SITUATIONS LEN5:
Broadridge Financial Solutions at $174.39 (after hours), +$6.65 / +3.96% today, runner-up of fifty-one, sends the ballot when a company you own through a broker calls a vote. This Len5 wants settled earning power bought cheaply, and settled means fees billed again every year: $4.9B of recurring revenue, +8% in the year to June 30, record signings of $305M, at about 18 times the $9.60 it earned with one-off items set aside, 31.8% under last September's high. WATCH next Monday, September 21, when comments close on a Securities and Exchange Commission proposal to make electronic delivery the default instead of paper - postage is the risk. VERDICT: a record year at a third off.

GROWTH LEN5:
ServisFirst Bancshares at $42.30 (after hours), +$0.17 / +0.40% today, runner-up of thirty, lends to businesses and well-off households across the South with almost no branches - 666 people running a $4.6B company. This Len5 wants profit growth the price has not already charged for, and none of this was bought: July 20 brought net income of $85.8M against $61.4M, +39.7%, loans up $532.6M in three months, and a net interest margin - what a bank keeps on loans after paying depositors - of 3.63%, wider by 0.53 points in a year, at 14.4 times profit. WATCH whether that loan pace holds once the margin stops widening, tentatively October 19. RISK: lending aimed at the fastest-growing states turns first when those states cool. VERDICT: 40% growth at an ordinary price.

HYPERGROWTH LEN5:
AppLovin at $333.05 (after hours), +$9.09 / +2.81% today, runner-up of thirty, runs the system that decides which advert appears inside a mobile app, and does it with 898 people. This Len5 wants a business early as well as fast. Fast is settled: August 5 brought revenue of $1.92B, +53%, and cash profit before interest, tax and wear on equipment of $1.61B - 84 cents of every revenue dollar. Early is the half holding it back, since a $111.8B company is what rivals try to displace. The figure to sit with is the beat itself: $3.76 a share against $3.75 carried, one cent, after 20, 7, 31 and 12 cents in the four quarters before it. VERDICT: growing 53% and clearing its own bar by less each time, $4.01 carried for November 4.

INCOME LEN5:
Euroseas at $74.80 (after hours), +$0.24 / +0.32% today, runner-up of thirty, owns 21 containerships and rents them out on charters measured in years. This Len5 wants cash reaching owners that the business itself funds, and the cover is close to absurd: the August 13 quarter earned $4.70 a share against $4.29 carried, while the dividend is $0.80 - about 17 cents of every dollar earned. That is $3.20 a year, near 4.3% here, paid on Wednesday. What holds it a step back is the building program: twelve more ships by 2029, taking the fleet from 21 to 33, out of that same cash. RISK: only 2.6M of its 6.6M shares trade freely, so a handful of orders sets the price.

Five of these six are arguments about a business. Personalis is not one any more: its worth was settled in a document on July 20, and the only say its owners have left is a vote with no date on it. Sixteen closes out of seventeen say they think the number in that document is wrong. Nobody has offered them a better one.

text:
The post uses a single family photo at a roller rink as visual proof that skipping all childhood vaccines produces healthy kids and that listed ingredients are unnecessary. Anecdotes like this circulate widely in certain circles because healthy unvaccinated children exist, yet they cannot establish population-level safety or necessity; families who remain unvaccinated often differ in diet, healthcare-seeking, and exposure patterns from the general population.

Aluminum salts appear as adjuvants in several routine vaccines (DTaP, hepatitis B, HPV, pneumococcal) at microgram-to-low-milligram levels per dose—amounts well below typical daily dietary intake from food and water. Thimerosal (ethylmercury) was largely removed from U.S. and European childhood schedules two decades ago and remains only in some multi-dose flu vials; it is chemically distinct from the methylmercury found in fish. Formaldehyde is used to inactivate viruses or toxins and leaves residual traces smaller than those naturally present in a pear or apple. Polysorbate 80 functions as an emulsifier and is a common food additive found in ice cream at far higher concentrations. Fetal-cell-line claims refer to the WI-38 and MRC-5 cell lines derived from two elective abortions in the 1960s; these immortalized cell cultures are used to grow certain viruses during manufacturing (rubella, varicella, and others), but the finished vaccine contains neither fetal cells nor tissue.

The author’s bio and repeated posts rest on virus denialism drawn from Stefan Lanka and Thomas Cowan. Lanka’s 2011 prize offer for measles-virus proof produced a German civil case that turned on the wording of the contest (one paper versus six papers), not on scientific existence; appellate judges explicitly stated that the ruling said nothing about whether the virus exists and noted the scientific consensus that it does. Cowan, who surrendered his California medical license, has promoted terrain theory, 5 G as the cause of COVID, and the view that viruses are cellular waste rather than pathogens. Viruses including measles, polio, and SARS-CoV-2 have been isolated in culture, independently sequenced by many labs, visualized by electron microscopy, and shown to meet adapted Koch-style criteria through animal models and controlled challenge studies.

Large-scale data show vaccines have averted an estimated 154 million deaths since 1974, with the largest gains among infants. Unvaccinated children experience higher rates of the targeted diseases (measles, pertussis, etc.). Observational comparisons of vaccinated versus unvaccinated children for chronic conditions (asthma, developmental delay, allergies) yield mixed results; some smaller practice-based studies report higher odds in the vaccinated group, while larger representative surveys, such as Germany’s KiGGS, find little difference once vaccine-preventable illnesses are excluded. Confounding by lifestyle, diagnostic intensity, and socioeconomic factors remains difficult to eliminate in non-randomized data.

text:
Randi — I admire what you’re doing to advance crypto education and adoption across the Far East. That region will matter, and voices that can explain digital assets clearly, without the usual noise, are scarce. Keep going. 

Exercise utmost caution with Hong Kong and other regions under Beijing’s control. While Hong Kong appears open on paper—with licenses, conferences, and headlines branding it as “Asia’s crypto hub”—the legal and political landscape has changed over the past decade. Rules can change suddenly, data and devices are vulnerable, and content creators or educators do not have any special exemptions. This isn’t a call to abandon Asia, but rather a warning not to regard Hong Kong as a low-risk location. 

Japan and South Korea are the more promising options for the work you genuinely want to pursue. Japan features a solid regulatory framework, established exchanges, and institutions familiar with handling crypto publicly. South Korea boasts strong retail interest and a market that values compliance highly. Both countries offer opportunities to develop relationships without the heavy political burden. 

Speaking from personal experience, not as a pundit, I spent time in that neighborhood during an Air Force overseas tour in Okinawa. We frequently encountered Chinese and North Korean fighter jets—mainly MiGs—posing a consistent harassment threat to U.S. and allied forces in the region. This wasn't just theory; it was operational reality. I advise you to avoid entering environments where the risks are both political and personal, beyond mere market fluctuations. 

Finally, stay visible and stay ambitious, but choose jurisdictions that let you work safely and return home without harm. Japan and Korea are better suited to that goal than Hong Kong. Take care of yourself.

📢Here is the latest Per AI on the #ClarityACT Changes. 📢

H.R. 3633 — Complete Verified Change List: June 1 Reported → September 13 Latest

Old: Senate Banking reported bill (BILLS-119hr3633rs, June 1, 2026) New: Latest substitute draft (EHF26724, September 13, 2026; 635 pp, 4 divisions, 101 sections)

How this was produced. 

Both bills were segmented into sections and matched by number (RS §104 → new §10104, and so on). Every one of the 62 carried-over sections was compared at the character level with dollar amounts, percentages, and deadlines preserved, so a changed number cannot hide. The June 1 side is clean XML; the September 13 side is text extracted from the PDF with the line-number margin removed by x-coordinate. Quoted passages below are lightly normalized for readability (smart-quotes and PDF hyphenation artifacts repaired); wording is verbatim.

Confidence. 

This pass specifically re-checked the sections an earlier, coarser diff had called "unchanged," and it caught two real edits those had missed (§102 and §509). A final sweep then scanned every carried-over section for residual word-level changes — modal swaps ("shall"→"may"), small clause replacements, single-word edits — after filtering out the three benign transforms (act→division, cross-reference renumbering, PDF hyphenation). It found no further substantive change: the only residuals are the reference plumbing noted in Part 1 and extraction noise (sequential line numbers, next-title headers crossing section boundaries). Sections not listed in Part 3 are substantively unchanged apart from the systemic renumbering.

One limit. 

Everything here is June 1 → September 13. It cannot be split at the July 22 draft (EHF26654), which was never provided as a file.

Part 1 — One systemic change touching most sections

The bill was reorganized from a single run of titles into four divisions (A–D). As a mechanical consequence, two things changed in nearly every section:

"this Act" became "this division" or "division B" wherever a cross-reference now points into the newly separated CFTC division.

Internal cross-references were renumbered to the 5-digit scheme (e.g. a reference to "section 104" became "section 10104," "section 601" became "section 10601").

Some references gained "as amended by this Act" / "as added or amended by" — pointing at the Commodity Exchange Act text that Division B now supplies (e.g. §501, §902, §111). Same plumbing category; not a policy change.

Plainspeak: Bills reference their own sections constantly ("as required under section 104…"). When a bill is carved into separate divisions, every one of those internal pointers has to be re-aimed, and any reference that reaches into the new CFTC division has to say "this division" instead of "this Act." That is why almost every section shows some text change: it is the bookkeeping of the reorganization, not a decision to regulate anything differently. It is spelled out once here so that in the section-by-section list below, a flagged change can be read as real policy rather than this background renumbering.

Part 2 — The biggest change: an entire section replaced

§904 → §11004 — Build Now Act removed, GENIUS Act corrections inserted

Similarity 0.05. This is a wholesale swap, not an edit.

OLD (June 1): "SEC. 904. Build Now Act. (a) Definitions. In this section: (1) Covered recipient. The term 'covered recipient' means a metropolitan city or urban county … as defined in section 102 of the Housing [and Community Development Act] …" — roughly 1,270 words of community-development housing policy.

NEW (Sept 13): "SEC. 11004. Technical corrections to the GENIUS Act. (a) Credit Union Parity.—The GENIUS Act (12 U.S.C. 5901 et seq.) is amended— (1) in section 2 …" — technical and conforming amendments to the stablecoin statute.

Plainspeak: The June 1 bill carried a passenger that had nothing to do with digital assets — the "Build Now Act," a block of housing and community-development policy directing money to metropolitan cities and urban counties. Riders like that are usually attached to buy a vote or move a bill along. It has been cut entirely. The slot it occupied is now filled with housekeeping fixes to the GENIUS Act (the 2025 federal stablecoin law): conforming tweaks and, notably, "credit union parity" language so credit unions are treated on equal footing with banks under that statute. So this is two moves in one — an unrelated policy rider removed, and a set of technical corrections to the stablecoin law added in its place.

Part 3 — Substantive edits inside carried-over sections

§2 → §10001 — Definitions
Digital commodity, OLD: "…the meaning given the term in section 1a of the Commodity Exchange Act (7 U.S.C. 1a), as added by this Act."

Digital commodity, NEW: "…section 1a of the Commodity Exchange Act (7 U.S.C. 1a), as amended by division B…"

NEW definition added: "Decentralized finance trading protocol.—Except where otherwise expressly provided, the term 'decentralized finance trading protocol' has the meaning given the term in section 1a of the Commodity Exchange Act…"

The decentralized-governance / control wording was also tightened (a phrase changed to "unilateral").

Plainspeak: "Digital commodity" is the hinge term that decides which tokens fall under the CFTC's commodity regime versus the SEC's securities regime. The June 1 bill defined it by pointing at a piece of the Commodity Exchange Act that it said this law would create — but the text that was supposed to create it wasn't actually in the bill. It was a definition pointing at a blank. The fix routes the pointer to Division B, the new CFTC title that does supply that text, so the definition now resolves to something real. The bill also adds a formal definition of "decentralized finance trading protocol" (the software that lets people trade tokens without a middleman) using the same routing, and it tightened the language on when a DeFi system counts as controlled by an identifiable group — a change flagged by the word "unilateral," which narrows control to a party that can act on its own. Whether a protocol is "controlled" is what determines if anyone can be held responsible for it, so that wording is consequential even though it's a few words.

§102 → §10102 — Disclosure requirements (the ancillary-asset core)

NEW subsection added: "Rule of Construction.—Nothing in this Act, or any rule or regulation promulgated under this Act, may be construed to result in an ancillary asset not being treated as a network token."

Plainspeak: The whole point of the "network token / ancillary asset" framework is to give a token a path out of full securities regulation. This adds a belt-and-suspenders instruction to regulators and courts: nothing in the Act or its rules can be read to knock an ancillary asset out of "network token" status. In practice it's a thumb on the scale against an interpretation — by the SEC or a court — that would use some other provision to pull a token back under tighter securities treatment. It doesn't create a new right or obligation; it locks in how the existing ones are read. (For the record, the 12-month and 60-day disclosure clocks in this section are identical in both drafts — those were extraction artifacts, not changes.)

§203 → §10203 — Preventing Illicit Finance Through Partnership Act

NEW recipient added to information-sharing: "…and (D) any Federal, State, or local law enforcement agency or office of an attorney general of a State that the Secretary of the Treasury, in consultation with the Director [designates]…" Also adds a 14-day element.

Plainspeak: This section sets up a formal channel for the government and private firms (exchanges, banks) to trade tips about illicit crypto activity — money laundering, sanctions evasion, fraud. June 1 kept that channel largely federal. September 13 widens the circle of who can be brought in to include state attorneys general and state and local police, and adds a 14-day timing element. The effect is more cops at the table: state-level enforcers get access to the same information-sharing partnership, not just Treasury and federal agencies. It's part of a consistent thread across several sections (see §204 and §309) pulling state and local enforcement into the regime.

§204 → §10204 — Financial Technology Protection Act

NEW list entries: "(vi) State financial regulators. (vii) State or local law enforcement agencies."

Plainspeak: Same direction of travel as §203, in a different section. A designated list of bodies — the entities meant to be looped in under the Financial Technology Protection Act — now expressly includes state financial regulators and state or local law enforcement. On its own it's a two-line addition, but together with §203 and §309 it shows the September draft deliberately writing state and local enforcers into the digital-asset framework wherever the June bill had named mostly federal players.

§205 → §10205 — Digital asset kiosks

NEW consumer protection: "Right to Cancel.—With respect to a transaction that is subject to the restriction under paragraph (1), the new customer … shall have the right, at any time before the expiration of the 72-hour period described in that paragraph, to cancel that transaction and receive [a refund]…"

Plainspeak: "Digital asset kiosks" are crypto ATMs — the machines in gas stations and convenience stores that let people buy or send crypto with cash. They're a notorious vector for scams, especially against older people who are talked into feeding cash into one by a fraudster on the phone. The bill already put restrictions on first-time customers; this adds a concrete escape hatch: a new customer can cancel the transaction any time within a 72-hour window and get their cash back. In plain terms, it's a cooling-off / refund right aimed squarely at giving scam victims a chance to undo the transfer before the money is gone.

§308 → §10308 — Risk management standards for digital asset intermediaries

Covered activity expanded, NEW: "…risk-based capability to detect market manipulation, fraud, cyber intrusions, money laundering…" plus reworded activity descriptions ("display of trading interest, entering orders"; "effecting transactions").

Plainspeak: This section tells digital-asset intermediaries (the trading platforms and similar firms) what they must be able to watch for and manage as a condition of operating. The September draft broadens that duty in two ways: it adds "cyber intrusions" to the list of things a firm must have a risk-based capability to detect (alongside manipulation, fraud, and money laundering), and it rewords the description of covered trading activity — "display of trading interest, entering orders," "effecting transactions" — so the obligations reach the full mechanics of running a market, not just a narrower slice. The upshot is a somewhat higher and more explicit bar for what these firms' internal controls have to cover, hacking included.

§309 → §10309 — Study on digital asset mixers and tumblers

NEW consultation requirement: "…in consultation with the Attorney General and State and local law enforcement agencies, submit to the Committee on Banking…"

Plainspeak: "Mixers and tumblers" are services that pool and shuffle crypto to break the on-chain trail between sender and receiver — privacy tools that are also heavily used to launder stolen or sanctioned funds. The bill orders a government study of their illicit use. The September change requires that study to be produced in consultation with the Justice Department and state and local law enforcement, rather than by the financial regulators alone. Same state/local-enforcement thread as §203 and §204, applied here to who helps shape the research and, by extension, any recommendations that flow from it.

§401 → §10401 — Permissibility of digital asset activities (banking)

NEW coverage of credit unions: adds defined terms including "'State credit union supervisor' has the meaning given the term in section 6003 of the Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2020 (31 U.S.C. 5311 note)" and federal-credit-union language. +291 words.

Plainspeak: This section spells out which digital-asset activities regulated financial institutions are actually allowed to do — custody, stablecoin handling, and the like. As written in June, it was framed around banks. The September draft brings credit unions explicitly into the same permission structure, adding the definitions needed to do so (including "State credit union supervisor," borrowed from the Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2020). Credit unions are member-owned and separately regulated by the NCUA, so if the bill had stayed bank-only they'd have been left guessing about whether they could offer the same crypto services. This closes that gap and lets the credit-union system play on the same field as banks. It pairs with the "credit union parity" fix over in §11004.

§404 → §10404 — Prohibiting interest and yield on payment stablecoins

NEW "regulatory circuit breaker" with a community-bank carve-out: "…the term 'community bank' means a depository institution, or depository institution holding company, with total consolidated assets of less than $10,000,000,000. … Determination by Secretary; Regulations.— If, not later than 18 months after the [date]…" +225 words.

Plainspeak: This is the provision that bars paying interest or yield just for holding a stablecoin — the Tillis–Alsobrooks compromise. The worry behind it is that if stablecoins paid interest like a savings account, people would pull deposits out of community banks and into crypto, draining the funding those banks lend against. The September draft adds a new safety valve aimed at exactly that fear: a "regulatory circuit breaker" pegged to "community banks," defined here as institutions under $10 billion in assets, with the Treasury Secretary directed to act within an 18-month window. In plain terms, it's a monitoring-and-intervention mechanism so that if the stablecoin rules start pulling money away from smaller banks, there's a defined trigger to respond — a concession to community-bank interests that wasn't in the June text.

§509 → §10509 — AI innovation labs

DELETED (June 1 only): "After the expiration of the 120-day extension period, if the agency has not made a determination on the application, the application will automatically be deemed approved and effective." This sentence is removed in September 13.
A mandatory "shall" was also softened to "may" in this section.

Plainspeak: This section sets up "innovation labs" where financial regulators let firms test AI-driven products under supervision, with a clock on how long the agency can take to approve a test project. The June draft had a sharp backstop: if the regulator sat past the extended 120-day deadline, the project was automatically deemed approved — inaction meant yes. September 13 deletes that. Now agency silence no longer greenlights a project; approval has to be affirmative. Combined with a "shall" softened to "may" elsewhere in the section, the change shifts power back toward the regulators — firms lose the automatic win they'd get from a missed deadline. If you build in this space, this is the one to watch: the default flipped from "approved unless the agency acts" to "not approved until the agency acts."

§601 → §10601 — Protecting software developers

Restructured and cut by ~203 words; the inline decentralized-finance-trading-protocol developer language was trimmed. CFTC-side developer protection now also lives in Division B §20209.

Plainspeak: This is the provision meant to protect people who write blockchain software but don't custody anyone's funds — the "I just publish code" defense — from being regulated as if they were financial intermediaries. On the securities side (§10601) it was trimmed by about 203 words. The reason it shrank rather than weakened: the parallel protection for the commodity side now lives in the new CFTC division at §20209. So the developer shield wasn't cut — it was split, with the securities half staying here and the commodity half moving to Division B. To know the true scope of protection now, you have to read both sections together rather than this one alone.

§604 → §10604 — Blockchain Regulatory Certainty Act

Defined term narrowed, OLD: "'developer or provider' … means any person or business that creates or publishes software to facilitate the creation of, or provide maintenance to, a distributed ledger…"

NEW: "'blockchain developer' … means any person or business that creates or publishes software to facilitate the creation of, or provide maintenance to, a distributed ledger…"(−89 words overall; the "or provider" branch was removed and definitions reworked.)

Plainspeak: The Blockchain Regulatory Certainty Act is a liability shield for people who build or run blockchain infrastructure without controlling customer money. Who exactly gets that shield depends entirely on the defined term. June 1 protected a "developer or provider." September 13 renames the category to "blockchain developer" and drops the separate "provider" branch, reworking the definition. The practical effect is a narrower gate: some actors who would have qualified as a "provider" may no longer fit under "blockchain developer." So this is a real tightening of who's covered, not just a relabel — worth reading the full new definition before assuming a given role still qualifies.

§306 → §10306 — Voluntary cybersecurity program (DeFi)

The inline definition of "decentralized finance trading protocol" was removed (that term is now defined centrally in §10001), with a cross-reference added. −33 words.

Plainspeak: Housekeeping, not policy. The term "decentralized finance trading protocol" used to be defined again inside this section; now that it's defined once, centrally, in §10001, the local copy was deleted and replaced with a pointer to the central definition. The voluntary cybersecurity program itself works the same as before — this just removes a duplicated definition so there's a single source of truth for the term.

§906 → §40101 — Effective date

OLD: "SEC. 906. Effective date. This Act, and the amendments made by this Act, shall take effect on the date that is 360 days after … except that, if a provision … requires a [rulemaking, on publication of the final rule]…"

NEW: restructured into "(a) In General … shall take effect on the date that is 360 days after … (b) Rulemaking provisions … on the date on which the final rule implementing that provision is published." Moved into its own Division D.

Plainspeak: This is the "when does the law switch on" clause. The core timing is unchanged — most of the Act takes effect 360 days after enactment, and provisions that need a rulemaking switch on when that final rule publishes. What changed is drafting hygiene: the June version buried the rulemaking carve-out in an "except that" tail; the September version breaks it into clean "(a) in general" and "(b) rulemaking provisions" subsections and moves the whole thing into its own Division D. No date moved; it's just written more clearly and relocated.

Part 4 — Wholly new material (no June 1 counterpart)

These are entirely new relative to the reported bill. Because Division B alone runs to hundreds of pages, this lists the sections and what they do rather than quoting each in full.

Division A, Title IX — Law Enforcement Tools (new)

§10901 Guarding Unprotected Aging Retirees from Deception (GUARD) — elder-fraud focus.
§10902 Grant program for State and local digital asset enforcement.
§10903 Digital asset law enforcement and national security training program.
§10904 Establishment of a digital asset cyber innovation center.
§10905 Strengthening agency frameworks for enforcement.
§10906 Compliance with lawful orders requiring reissuance.

Plainspeak: An entirely new enforcement toolkit that didn't exist in the June bill. It does four practical things: creates elder-fraud protections aimed at the scams that target older people (the "GUARD" section, which connects to the crypto-ATM cancel right in §205); sends federal grant money and training to state and local police so they can actually investigate crypto crime, which most don't have the tooling for today; stands up a "cyber innovation center" as a technical hub; and addresses "reissuance" — the messy situation where a court orders stolen or frozen tokens to be re-minted or reassigned to their rightful owner, and firms need legal cover to comply. Taken together, it's the bill leaning into enforcement and victim recovery, and it's the clearest expression of the state-and-local-enforcement thread that also shows up in §§203, 204, and 309.

Division B — Digital Commodity Intermediaries Act (new; the CFTC regime)

Titles XI–XII, §§20001–20219. Restores the CFTC registration framework the reported bill had deleted: definitions under the Commodity Exchange Act (§20101, the text §10001 now points to), jurisdiction, trading certification, and registration/regulation of digital commodity exchanges (§20204), qualified custodians (§20205), brokers and dealers (§20206), associated persons, and pool operators/advisors. Includes items the original House bill never had: software-developer protections (§20209), portfolio margining (§20211), a digital commodity retail advocate (§20213), protection of self-custodied digital assets (§20216), and trading reports (§20215).

Plainspeak: This is the single largest addition, and it's the other half of the whole regulatory design. A digital asset can be a security (SEC's turf) or a commodity (CFTC's turf). The June bill built out the SEC side but left the CFTC side as an empty promise — it kept referring to CFTC registration rules that weren't written down anywhere in the text (that's the dangling definition from §10001). Division B is those missing rules: it defines the terms, sets the CFTC's jurisdiction, and lays out who has to register and how — the exchanges where digital commodities trade, the custodians who hold them, the brokers and dealers who intermediate, the pool operators and advisors. It also adds consumer-facing pieces the original House bill never had: a "digital commodity retail advocate" (an ombudsman for ordinary customers), an explicit right to self-custody your own assets, and public trading reports. In short, this is what makes the two-regulator system actually function instead of pointing at a hole — and structurally, it's Senate Agriculture's jurisdiction being stitched into Senate Banking's bill.

Verification note: this is confirmed as wholly new against June 1, and the section list is read from the text, but the ~29 section bodies here were not read line by line — see Part 7.

Division C — Ethics Requirements for Digital Assets (new)

§§30101–30104. Codifies the rules into 5 U.S.C. Chapter 131, new Subchapter IV (§§13151–13154):
Covered individuals (§13151): public officials and employees; anyone elected President, Vice President, or to Congress but not yet sworn in; and their spouses.

Significant financial interest: ≥ $15,000 of equity (inflation-adjusted) in an entity that drew a plurality of revenue from issuing or sponsoring digital assets in the prior 3 years.

The ban (§13152): a covered individual may not, for consideration, issue or sponsor a digital asset, or maintain a significant financial interest (with exceptions); interests must be divested or placed in a qualified blind trust.

Enforcement: by the U.S. Attorney General, civil action in district court; penalty is disgorgement plus the greater of 4% of the consideration or $500,000.

No sunset or severability sections (the July draft's standalone sunset was dropped).

Plainspeak: This is the conflict-of-interest division, and it's the politically hottest part of the bill — the response to concern about federal officials profiting from crypto ventures while in power. It bars "covered individuals" — federal officials and employees, people elected to the presidency, vice presidency, or Congress but not yet sworn in, and their spouses — from three things: launching a token for money ("issue"), lending their name or office to promote one ("sponsor"), or holding a meaningful financial stake in a crypto-issuing business (roughly $15,000+ of equity in an entity that makes most of its money issuing or sponsoring digital assets). Those with such a stake have to sell it or move it into a blind trust. Two design choices matter most. First, enforcement runs through the U.S. Attorney General only — not state attorneys general — which is the compromise that reportedly kept Republican negotiators on board and that some Democrats objected to as too weak.

text:
The cleanest answer is: almost none that look like a long, unilateral, unverifiable pause in a winner-take-all race. Game theory is not a slogan; it is a description of incentives. When the payoff to being first is large, compliance is hard to monitor, and the game has an absorbing “someone crosses the finish line” state, the Nash outcome is race. That is the default in military technology, most dual-use platforms, and commercial platform races.

There are cases where innovators or strategists deliberately slowed or constrained a method and were not immediately rolled. They share a pattern: the pause was short, the people who actually held the frontier coordinated, or the “win” was not winner-take-all because the downside was a shared commons. Those are the exceptions, not the rule.

### The best single example: recombinant DNA, 1974–1975
In July 1974 Paul Berg and colleagues published an open letter calling for a voluntary moratorium on the riskiest recombinant-DNA experiments (certain cloning of toxin or tumor-virus genes into *E. coli*). The fear was laboratory-created pathogens that could escape. The pause was widely observed in academic *and* industrial labs. No known violations.

They used the pause to hold the Asilomar conference (February 1975), invent containment categories, and hand NIH a framework. Guidelines appeared in 1976. Research resumed under rules. The field did not stall. Genentech was founded in 1976. The United States and Western Europe commercialized the technology and dominated the industry that followed. Hundreds of millions of experiments later, the original catastrophe scenarios did not materialize.

Did a competitor “overwhelm” them? The Soviet Union later ran a secret offensive biological-weapons program that used recombinant methods (Biopreparat / FERMENT). That is the game-theory objection in miniature: a state actor defected on the weapons side. It did not, however, seize the civilian scientific or industrial lead. The pause was months, not years; the people who could actually do the work were in the room; and the commercial prize was not “first lab to release a novel organism wins the world.”

That is the closest historical analog people reach for when they talk about an AI pause. It is also a limited analog. Capabilities were far more concentrated, the work was still mostly academic, and the pause was not a ban on the entire research program.

### A second, different kind of success: Montreal Protocol (CFCs)
CFCs were a profitable, mature industrial technology. The 1987 Montreal Protocol required countries and firms to phase them out. Production was not “paused pending safety research”; it was scheduled for elimination. Industry developed substitutes. Ozone-depleting substance production fell ~99%. The ozone layer is recovering. Firms that invested in alternatives were not displaced by holdouts; the holdouts were legally and commercially boxed in.

This worked because (1) substitutes existed or could be developed at acceptable cost, (2) the harm was a global commons everyone could measure, and (3) the agreement had nearly universal participation plus a multilateral fund for developing countries. It is coordination plus technology substitution, not a unilateral R&D freeze.

### Cases that look like restraint but do not refute the user’s point
- **Nuclear testing moratoria** (1958–61, later the Limited Test Ban, later the CTBT regime). Labs kept designing with simulations and stockpile stewardship. The weapons programs did not stop. When the Soviets broke the 1958–61 moratorium, the U.S. resumed.
- **U.S. offensive biological-weapons program** (Nixon, 1969) plus the 1972 Biological Weapons Convention. The U.S. walked away from an offensive capability. The USSR cheated for years. The U.S. was not “overwhelmed” in the sense of being conquered by bioweapons, but that is because the taboo, delivery problems, and mutual vulnerability are different from a capability race with a clear first-mover prize.
- **Tokugawa Japan and firearms** (17th–19th centuries). After mastering guns in the Sengoku period, the shogunate tightly controlled manufacture and ownership to lock in internal order. It delivered 250 years of domestic peace. Internal competitors did not overthrow the regime with better guns. The cost appeared later: when Perry arrived in 1853 the hardware lag was obvious, and Japan then modernized at extraordinary speed. Restraint served one strategic goal (internal monopoly on violence) until the external game changed.

### What these cases actually show
They do **not** show that “slowing down is usually fine.” They show the conditions under which slowing is not suicide:

1. The relevant actors who can actually advance the frontier are few and can talk to each other.
2. The pause is short and used to write rules or invent substitutes, not to freeze the field indefinitely.
3. Verification or social enforcement among insiders is possible.
4. The private prize for defecting is smaller than the shared cost of a disaster *or* a treaty changes the payoffs.
5. The technology is not already an instrument of great-power military competition with an absorbing end-state.

AI development in 2026 fails several of those tests at once: capabilities are spreading, the commercial and military prizes are enormous, verification of training runs and weights is hard, and at least one major state competitor has no incentive to accept a Western-led pause. That is why the prisoner’s-dilemma framing keeps winning the argument even among people who think the risks are real. Anthropic’s own move from a unilateral halt pledge to a “only if others verifiably slow too” policy is the game theory becoming explicit.

So the user’s challenge stands for the thing people usually mean by “slow down AI”: a durable, poorly verified, largely unilateral restraint while others keep training. History does not offer a comforting example of that working. It offers examples of *coordinated, time-bounded, rules-producing* restraint that then allowed the field to proceed. Those are different policies. Treating them as the same is how the debate talks past itself.

#TANZANIA: THE STATE MUST ANSWER: WHERE IS EMMANUEL NCHIMBI? A FORMER VICE-PRESIDENT CANNOT SIMPLY DISAPPEAR INTO SILENCE:

A former Vice-President of the United Republic of Tanzania has vanished from public life, and a State that claims the mantle of constitutional order has so far offered no independently verifiable answer to a question that now belongs to the law, not to rumour: where is Emmanuel John Nchimbi, and is he free? 

A man who has served as Member of Parliament, Deputy Minister, Minister of Information, Culture and Sports, Minister of Home Affairs, ambassador to Brazil and Egypt, Secretary-General of Chama Cha Mapinduzi, and, from 3 November 2025, Vice-President of the Union, is not a private citizen whose silence may be treated as a lifestyle choice.

On 24 July 2026 he publicly urged Tanzanians to continue demanding a new Constitution, one that would serve not only material development but the dignity and human worth of every person.

Within weeks of that appeal, the political machinery around him moved with a speed that would be remarkable in any functioning democracy and is, in this one, a warning.

The surrounding record is not conjecture. The general election of 29 October 2025 was followed by an internet shutdown, lethal force and a human-rights catastrophe that even the government-appointed Commission of Inquiry chaired by retired Chief Justice Mohamed Chande Othman could not conceal. 

That Commission recorded at least 518 deaths, 490 men, 28 women, 21 children, most of them unnatural; 197 victims died of gunshot wounds; thousands more were injured. 

The Commission itself conceded that the true number of dead may be higher because some victims were buried without passing through official mortuaries. 

Credible reporting and testimony from families, medical personnel and human-rights monitors indicate that both the dead and the disappeared exceed the Commission’s published count. 

Yet even for those deaths the State itself has formally acknowledged, there has been no transparent criminal accountability: no named perpetrators brought before an independent court, no public accounting that would allow the bereaved to know who fired, who ordered, and who buried the truth with the bodies. 

@Reuters reported allegations that security forces shot unarmed civilians. Human-rights organisations demanded independent investigation. What Tanzania has instead is an official minimum that already shames the Republic and a continuing refusal to do justice even for that minimum.

Against that blood-stained backdrop, Nchimbi’s subsequent treatment cannot be reduced to ordinary party discipline. After MwanaHALISI published a report headed “Nchimbi Agoma Kujiuzulu,” alleging that the Vice-President was resisting pressure to resign, the newspaper’s licence was suspended for six months on 19 August 2026 for alleged breaches of accuracy, balance and verification a sanction whose proportionality media stakeholders immediately questioned. 

On 25 August 2026 Nchimbi posted a letter announcing his resignation, to take effect on 4 September, and his intention to retire from politics and public service. The following day CCM expelled him. Energy Minister Deogratius Ndejembi was nominated and sworn in with extraordinary haste. 

The Attorney-General later told Parliament that Nchimbi had already ceased to hold office on 26 August upon loss of party membership. He was not publicly present at the installation of his successor. 

Former Prime Minister Joseph Sinde Warioba has stated that he spoke to Nchimbi by telephone on the day of the resignation letter, then could not reach him thereafter by call or message, and referred to reports still unverified that Nchimbi’s telephones may have been taken from him.

Those reports remain allegations. What is established is the sequence: public constitutional advocacy; a press sanction; a sudden resignation; expulsion; an instantaneous succession; and then silence.

Continued …
